source.author: Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville (drawing, 1859); from the certificate of addition to French patent no. 31470, preserved by INPI; scan via firstsounds.org
source.notes: Scott's own pen drawing of his phonautograph, the barrel-shaped horn, membrane and stylus writing on a soot-blackened paper wrapped round a hand-cranked cylinder, with his annotation 'Planche 1re annexée à ma demande du 29 juillet 1859 d'un certificat d'addition au brevet d'invention ... no 31470'. This is the model of the machine on which the 1860 'Au clair de la lune' sheet was made. object.medium: Phonautogram: sound-wave trace scratched by a stylus into lampblack on paper; recovered as audio in 2008
object.description: Seventeen years before Edison's phonograph, a Parisian typesetter and amateur scientist, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, built a machine that wrote sound down. His phonautograph gathered sound in a horn, let it shake a membrane, and had a hog's bristle scratch the vibration into lampblack on paper turning on a cylinder. Scott wanted a way to read speech from the squiggle; he never imagined playing it back. On 9 April 1860 he sang a few seconds of the folk song 'Au clair de la lune' into the horn and dated the sheet. In 2008 the First Sounds group had the trace scanned at high resolution and turned back into sound by computer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the thin, wavering voice that emerged is the oldest recording of a human voice that can be recognised. The drawing shown is Scott's own sketch of his machine from his 1859 patent papers. The visitor hears the eleven-second 2008 recovery.
facts: The sheet was deposited with the Académie des sciences in Paris in 1861 and lay unplayed for 147 years.
The first 2008 playback ran at the wrong speed and was taken for a girl's voice; correcting the cylinder speed revealed a slow male voice, probably Scott's own.
Scott patented the phonautograph on 25 March 1857; Edison's phonograph, the first machine that could play sound back, followed in 1877.
